faq.q: Can I give aspirin to a patient with suspected bleeding?

faq.a: Give oxygen, start IV fluids, and arrange urgent pericardiocentesis.
faq.q: What is the first step if I suspect cardiac tamponade?

faq.a: When PCI cannot be performed within 120 minutes and there are no contraindications to thrombolysis.

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer with crushing chest pain and hypotension arrives; what is your immediate management and why? — Give aspirin, oxygen, IV fluids, obtain ECG, consider thrombolysis if PCI unavailable; treat shock first.
How do you differentiate acute pulmonary embolism from severe pneumonia on bedside exam? — Look for pleuritic pain, clear lungs, RV dilation on ultrasound, and absence of fever.

A patient with known rheumatic mitral stenosis presents with sudden dyspnoea; what red‑flag complications must you rule out? — Pulmonary oedema, atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, and thrombo‑embolism.
Why is beta‑blocker contraindicated in a patient with acute decompensated heart failure? — It can worsen cardiac output by reducing contractility and heart rate.
What bedside ultrasound finding confirms cardiac tamponade? — Large pericardial effusion with right‑atrial collapse during inspiration.

In a hypertensive emergency with neurological symptoms, what is the target blood pressure and why? — Reduce MAP by no more than 25 % within the first hour, aiming for <140/90 mmHg to prevent cerebral injury.
Explain why streptokinase may be preferred over tenecteplase in a low‑resource setting. — It is cheaper, widely available, and does not require weight‑based dosing.
What are the key features that distinguish aortic dissection from myocardial infarction? — Tearing back pain, pulse deficit, widened mediastinum on X‑ray, and lack of ST‑elevation.
ai.title: Cardiovascular Emergencies
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Rapid identification and management of life‑threatening cardiac and vascular conditions in low‑resource settings. Focus on bedside assessment, pragmatic investigations and tiered treatment.

b: Key diagnoses: acute coronary syndrome, acute decompensated heart failure, hypertensive emergency, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, cardiac tamponade, severe arrhythmias.
sections.p: Sudden onset of cardiac or major vascular dysfunction that threatens organ perfusion or causes death if not treated within minutes to hours.

b: Shock stages: compensated (tachycardia, cool peripheries), decompensated (hypotension, altered mental status), irreversible (multi‑organ failure).
ACS risk: TIMI or GRACE scores if calculators available; otherwise use clinical high‑risk features (ST‑elevation, hypotension, heart failure).
sections.p: Severity is judged by hemodynamic compromise, organ dysfunction and response to initial therapy.

b: Ischemic: plaque rupture, coronary spasm, anemia, severe anemia (e.g., malaria, sickle cell).
Infectious: rheumatic fever, infective endocarditis (HIV, TB), pericardial TB.
Hypertensive: malignant hypertension, pheochromocytoma (rare).
Thrombo‑embolic: deep‑vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism (post‑surgery, immobilisation).
Structural: rheumatic mitral stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, congenital heart disease.
sections.p: Identify the precipitating pathology; in East Africa infectious and rheumatic diseases are common triggers.

b: Chest pain: crushing, radiating to left arm/jaw (ACS); tearing back pain (aortic dissection).
Dyspnoea with rales, raised JVP (acute heart failure, tamponade).
Palpitations, syncope (ventricular tachycardia, bradyarrhythmia).
Cold, clammy skin, oliguria (shock).
sections.p: Presenting features vary by organ involved but share sudden chest pain, dyspnoea, syncope or shock signs.
Prioritise bedside tools; use laboratory and imaging when available.

t.b: Is there myocardial ischaemia or arrhythmia? ST‑elevation, new LBBB, ventricular tachycardia guide urgent reperfusion or anti‑arrhythmic therapy.
Is the patient hypoxic or hypotensive? Guides oxygen, fluids, vasopressor need.
Is there pulmonary congestion, widened mediastinum, or pleural effusion? Helps differentiate heart failure, dissection, tamponade.
Is myocardial injury present? Positive supports ACS; negative does not exclude early MI.
Is there pericardial effusion, LV dysfunction, RV dilation? Detect tamponade, massive PE, severe LV failure.
Is thrombo‑embolism likely? High value supports PE; low value does not rule out in high‑risk patients.
Are electrolyte disturbances or hypoglycaemia contributing to arrhythmia? Correctable causes.

b: Persistent hypotension <90/60 mmHg despite fluids.
New or worsening arrhythmia with haemodynamic instability.
Cardiac tamponade signs: pulsus paradoxus, muffled heart sounds, JVD.
Aortic dissection with pulse deficit or neurological deficit.
Pulseless electrical activity or ventricular fibrillation.
Oxygen 6‑10 L/min via mask if SpO₂ <90 %.
Clopidogrel or ticagrelor added when PCI possible; avoid if active bleeding.
Heparin (unfractionated) for ACS or PE when coagulation monitoring available; avoid in severe thrombocytopenia.
Beta‑blocker (e.g., metoprolol) only after ruling out acute decompensated HF or bradycardia.
Nitrates for chest pain if SBP >100 mmHg; avoid in RV infarction.
Thrombolysis (streptokinase or tenecteplase) for STEMI or massive PE when PCI not feasible; contraindicated in recent surgery or bleeding.
Pericardiocentesis for tamponade using aseptic technique; if no echo, use clinical signs.
Urgent surgical referral for aortic dissection or ruptured aneurysm.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, stabilise circulation and oxygenation, then address secondary issues.

b: Refer for coronary angiography or cardiac surgery within 24‑48 h when indicated.
Start secondary‑prevention drugs (statin, ACE‑inhibitor, beta‑blocker) once stable.
Control hypertension, diabetes and HIV; counsel on smoking cessation and safe herbal use.
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce heart failure exacerbations.
sections.p: After stabilisation, arrange definitive care and secondary prevention.

b: Pulmonary infection causing pleuritic chest pain – differentiate by fever, cough, infiltrates on X‑ray.
Gastro‑oesophageal reflux – usually non‑radiating, no ECG changes.
Anxiety/panic attack – hyperventilation, normal vitals, no troponin rise.
Normal ECG early in MI – repeat after 15 min if suspicion remains.
Low troponin in renal failure – interpret trends, not single value.
D‑dimer elevated in infection or pregnancy – use clinical probability.

whenToSeekHelp: Chest pain with diaphoresis or radiating to arm/jaw
